This page contains a list of tools and commands I find particularly useful (particularly *outside* of work.)

## Reading and writing

- *Document writing*. I never got into the Microsoft Office suite of tools that includes Word. I've previously had to use Word for work a lot and I struggle to find much good to say about it. I do the majority of my writing for others (including this website and blog) in [Markdown](https://daringfireball.net/projects/Markdown/), or [Quarto](https://quarto.org), which is basically also Markdown! Some of the benefits of writing in Markdown are that it's intuitive, readable, flexible, future proof, interoperable with many other programmes, and it allows you to focus on content. Plus it's the *lingua franca* of AI, and it's now even [supported by Google Docs](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2026/10/preview-edit-and-collaborate-on-Markdown-files-natively-across-Drive-and-Docs.html) for collaborative editing! If I *really* need to get a Word document out of the end, I use either [Pandoc](http://pandoc.org/) or [Quarto](https://quarto.org). See [useful commands](#useful-terminal-commands) below for how to use this.
- *Note taking*. I store most of my notes in the truly excellent [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md/). Obsidian is a clean text Markdown-based note-taking system that separates the data (Markdown files) from the viewer/editor in a way that means you always stay in control of your own data. I've found Microsoft [OneNote](https://www.onenote.com/) to be good too, but it's a bit less configurable, even if the app support across surfaces is excellent.
- *Text editor*. I use Microsoft's [Visual Studio Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/) (with the Markdown all in one and Markdown preview enhanced extensions) and [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md/).
- *Writing papers*. For papers, I've switched to using Markdown/[Quarto](https://quarto.org). You can find a [cookie-cutter research template with paper and slides here](https://github.com/aeturrell/cookiecutter-research-project). You can insert figures, tables, *and* numbers into text, including in-line, so that the paper and slides can be completely updated if the results change. That makes it perfect for reproducible analytical pipelines. You can also export to LaTeX. I still use LaTeX from time to time. Although Visual Studio Code has a LaTeX editor that's very good, I use [TeXshop](https://pages.uoregon.edu/koch/texshop/) for LaTeX editing.
- *Reading papers*. I store papers in [Zotero](https://www.zotero.org/), which is an open source endeavour. You can support them by paying for their storage. They have an excellent iPad app too. Even better, [you can sync your papers and notes with Obsidian](../blog/posts/til-zotero-and-obsidian/index.md).

## Coding and development

- *Version control*. I use [git](https://git-scm.com/) and [GitHub](https://github.com/).
- *Development environment*. I use [Visual Studio Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/) for almost all code, including Python and R. (I wrote a post about how to set it up for R [here](../blog/posts/setting-up-r-in-vscode/index.md).) I also use Docker for development, including the excellent Visual Studio Code docker extensions.
- *Cloud compute*. When I need cloud capabilities, I mostly go for [Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/), connecting via Visual Studio Code remote (instructions in [this post](../blog/posts/visual-studio-code-in-the-cloud/index.md).)
- *Package manager*. To install things sensibly on a Mac, I use [Homebrew](https://brew.sh/).
- *Terminal*:
    - [ghostty](https://ghostty.org/) for my terminal
    - [ohmyzsh](https://ohmyz.sh/) for zsh configuration
    - [ohmyposh](https://ohmyposh.dev/) as a prompt engine
    - [lsd](https://github.com/lsd-rs/lsd) as a replacement for `ls`
    - [wget](https://www.gnu.org/software/wget/) for downloads
    - [ripgrep](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep) for text-in-file search
    - [llm](https://github.com/simonw/llm) to run local and remote large language models
    - [duckdb -ui](https://duckdb.org/2025/03/12/duckdb-ui) for exploring SQL databases
    - [ffmpeg](https://ffmpeg.org/) for converting audio and video
    - [imagemagick](https://imagemagick.org/) for working with image files
    - [f2](https://github.com/ayoisaiah/f2) for bulk renaming files
    - [Inkscape](https://inkscape.org/) on the command line, mainly for converting things to svg 
- *Programming language*. My default is Python, for a whole host of reasons, with, of course, some SQL. I am a huge convert to [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) and now use it to install Python, build packages, and manage repo packages.
- *Building Python packages*. There's [a template for that](https://github.com/aeturrell/cookiecutter-python-package)! 
- *Hardware*. I use a MacBook Pro with the M5 Max chip, which is an amazing laptop.

## Communication

- *Slide shows*. My preference is to use written notes over slide decks whenever possible (you can read a bit more about why [here](../blog/posts/managing-public-sector-knowledge/managing-public-sector-knowledge.qmd#notes-should-be-the-default-with-microsoft-powerpoint-presentations-only-by-exception)), following the [Amazon model](https://www.managementtoday.co.uk/why-amazon-banned-powerpoint/leadership-lessons/article/1689543). But you need a slide show now and again! If it's leaning toward a general audience and it covers a wide range of topics, I'll typically use [Keynote](https://www.apple.com/uk/keynote/). I know it isn't cross-platform, but you can create something that looks good in it quickly and easily—and you can export every stage of builds to PDF too. For giving talks on research papers, I used to reach for [beamer](https://ctan.org/pkg/beamer) and LaTeX but I now use [Quarto for slides](https://quarto.org/docs/presentations/) because everything can be programmatically re-generated if results change, it plays nicely with code chunks and code execution, and the HTML slides you can create are pretty nice. Again, check out the research project template [here](https://github.com/aeturrell/cookiecutter-research-project)
- *Website*. I use [Quarto](https://quarto.org/) and [Github pages](https://pages.github.com/), a powerful combination. For the website code, I'm indebted to [Andrew Heiss](https://www.andrewheiss.com/) for making the code for his website available.

## Misc

- For graphics, I normally go for [matplotlib](https://matplotlib.org/), which is so much more powerful than most people realise. All of the graphics in my book [The Star Builders](../thestarbuilders/thestarbuilders.qmd) were created using matplotlib. If I need a manual programme for graphics, I normally use [Inkscape](https://inkscape.org/), which is much better on Mac than it once was.
- I keep track of tasks with the excellent [Things](https://culturedcode.com/things/) (Mac).
- For fonts, [Nerd Fonts](https://www.nerdfonts.com/) is good, as are the [GitHub ones](https://github.com/githubnext/monaspace). For a much wider selection, there's always [Google Fonts](https://fonts.google.com/).

## Useful terminal commands

For most of these, you'll need to download the tools first.

### Pandoc

With Pandoc, a line

```bash
pandoc briefing.md -V geometry:margin=0.2in --standalone \
--bibliography references.bib --citeproc --csl=harvard.csl -o briefing.docx
```

applied to a file called "briefing.md", a bibtex file of references ("references.bib"), and a citation style (here "harvard.csl") will produce a Word document called "briefing.docx". It's fairly similar to using [Quarto to generate a Word document](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/ms-word.html). For more elaborate documents, like a book manuscript, I've created a couple of helper tools like [this quarto template](https://github.com/aeturrell/cookie-cutter-quarto-book-manuscript).

### Magic(k) to create webp files from PDFs

```bash
magick -density 300 your_pdf.pdf \
  -background white -alpha remove -alpha off \
  -define webp:lossless=true \
  output_image.webp
```

### Magic(k)ing .HEIC files to jpgs

```bash
magick mogrify -format jpg *.HEIC
```

### ffmpeg mov to mp4

```bash
ffmpeg -i input.mov output.mp4
```

### One-line PDF to text

```bash
uvx docling path-to-your-pdf
```

### One-line parquet file data summary

```bash
uvx skimpy some_data.parquet
```

### Find string in text files

eg for .qmd files only

```bash
rg "<phrase>" -g "*.qmd"
```

### Interactive search results found in text files

```bash
rg "import pandas" --type py | fzf
```

I usually have an alias for this, `rgf`. To set this up on Mac, you'll need to `brew install` [**rg**](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep), [**bat**](https://github.com/sharkdp/bat), and [**fzf**](https://github.com/junegunn/fzf). Then add the following to your `.zshrc` file, if you're using ZSH (amend according to your setup.) You can open the file in an editor with `code ~/.zshrc`. Then add this to the end of the file:

```bash
# ripgrep + fzf interactive search → VS Code
rgf() {
  local result
  result=$(
    rg --color=always --line-number --no-heading --smart-case "$@" |
      fzf --ansi \
          --delimiter : \
          --preview 'bat --color=always --highlight-line {2} --map-syntax "*.qmd:Markdown" {1}' \
          --preview-window 'up,60%,border-bottom,+{2}+3/3,~3'
  )
  if [[ -n "$result" ]]; then
    local file line
    file=$(echo "$result" | cut -d: -f1)
    line=$(echo "$result" | cut -d: -f2)
    code --goto "${file}:${line}"
  fi
}
```

Now you can use commands like

```bash
rgf "import pandas" -g "*.qmd"
```

to interactively, fuzzily, and quickly search your files.

### Bulk renaming

```bash
f2 -f '\(2021\)' -r '[2022]'
```

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
| ORIGINAL                             | RENAMED                              | STATUS |
| ************************************************************************************ |
| No Pressure (2021) S01.E01.2160p.mp4 | No Pressure [2022] S01.E01.2160p.mp4 | ok     |
| No Pressure (2021) S01.E02.2160p.mp4 | No Pressure [2022] S01.E02.2160p.mp4 | ok     |
| No Pressure (2021) S01.E03.2160p.mp4 | No Pressure [2022] S01.E03.2160p.mp4 | ok     |
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### System monitoring

Basic (built in):

```bash
top
```

Much more detail and easier to read (but requires install):

```bash
bpytop
```

## Pre-commit heroes

Some tools I've found useful as part of a [pre-commit configuration](https://pre-commit.com).

### Panache

"[Panache](https://panache.bz) is a language server, formatter, and linter for Quarto and other Markdown flavors, including Pandoc, R Markdown, and MyST. It is written in Rust and understands syntax that generic Markdown tools often miss, including fenced divs, tables, and math."

Panache does markdown + code block syntax formatting, which is why I like it. Unfortunately it doesn't currently support Jupyter notebooks.

### Ruff for Python formatting, linting, and sorting

Formatting:

```bash
ruff format path/to/code/
```

Linting

```bash
ruff check path/to/code/
```

Sorting imports

```bash
ruff check --select I --fix .
```

### Stripping output content from Jupyter notebooks

[NBStripout](https://github.com/kynan/nbstripout) is the tool for this!
